source.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
source.authors: Thomas F. Burns; T. Fukai; C. Earls

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own in-context-learning results, but it neither measures induction heads nor tests their formation, mechanism, or contribution to learning.
record.gate_note: The paper cites work on induction heads in its discussion of proposed explanations for ICL, but its experiments concern an associative-memory model and residual attention-value streams. It does not measure induction-head behavior, attention to the token after an earlier copy, or induction-head formation during training. Its ICL results are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study proposes residual attention streams (queries/keys/values added across layers) and reports ICL task accuracy and benchmark gains. It never measures induction heads, previous-token heads, induction attention patterns, head formation timing, or per-token in-context loss. Olsson et al. is cited only for background (ICL not usually seen in one-layer Transformers). Its results bear on an architecture modification, not on any version of the induction-head claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that an associative-memory-inspired residual value stream speeds ICL in a two-layer Transformer. They also report improved IOI and some benchmark performance at 8M and 1B scale. They acknowledge that the gains are modest and task-specific (minimal on PIQA/HellaSwag), the implementation is naive, and generalisability is uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces associative-memory-inspired residual streams between attention layers. It does not use the original induction-head measurement or intervention method.
record.method_sensitivity: The two-layer synthetic task results differ by residual-stream type: value and query streams reach the reported accuracy threshold earlier, while the key-stream comparison with Classic is reported as not significant. In the 1B evaluations, the authors report gains concentrated in ARC and OpenBookQA, with almost no change in PIQA and HellaSwag.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual value streams cut snapshots to 0.95 accuracy on IC from 64.5±5.12 to 49.0±2.12, and on IC2 from 63.25±4.15 to 47.75±1.3; the query stream also helps; the key stream is not significant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding cross-layer residual streams of attention values (or queries) speeds ICL acquisition in a two-layer Transformer on a synthetic classification task.

fits_no_version.finding: 8M toy LMs with residual value streams give ~41% correct IOI probability vs ~7% for Classic. A 1B model shows a clear IOI-Hard gain (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual value streams improve IOI-style in-context tasks in small language models despite near-identical training loss.

record.problems: The paper does not analyze induction heads, so its experiments cannot establish their presence or causal role. The IOI-Hard result is presented in a figure without numerical values in the text. The authors also note uncertain generalisability, task-specific gains, and a naïve residual-stream implementation.
record.rows_left_out: The IOI per-sentence probabilities in Table 2 and the 1B training-loss, benchmark-accuracy, and IOI-Hard curves in Figures 4–6 and 14 were not separately extracted. They concern general language-model performance rather than induction-head measurement; the aggregate IOI and IOI-Hard findings are represented in R9 and R10.

untested.parts: No mechanism analysis of heads or composition.
Training curves are task accuracy on a synthetic classification task; no induction-head formation, loss bump, or phase-change analysis.
No measure of how much ICL runs through induction heads.
No search for induction heads in any model.
Varies architecture, not data; no induction-head formation measured.
Few-shot benchmarks evaluated, but no attribution to heads.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is correct. The paper's synthetic task follows Reddy (2024), which is related to induction-head emergence. However, this paper never analyses heads, so no row bears on any version. The AMICL model's keys/queries mix each token with the previous token, which resembles a previous-token-plus-match induction algorithm. This is a hand-designed construction, not a measured finding about trained models.
